text: There is one question my guests ask me more than any other.
They sit in my majolis, they drink the coffee, they look around the house,
and then they ask me quietly, chic.
How does the money stay in your family while it slips out of everyone else's hands?
I always give the same answer.
It is not luck, and it is not a secret bank.
It is ten small things we do with money every single day,
and most people in America never even think about them.
One of them, number seven, made a visitor go completely silent for a full minute.
Stay until then, because it will change how you look at every dollar you earn.
Asterisk, my name is Umar. I am a chic from Dubai.
And I have sat in my majolis for more than 40 years,
listening to merchants, builders, farmers, and bankers.
Rich ones, and ruined ones.
After that long, you stop seeing money as numbers.
You see habits, and the habits of people who keep their wealth
are very different from the habits of people who lose it.
Asterisk, number one, we are paid for the value we create, not for the hours we sit.
Asterisk, when I was a young man,
my father took me to the old souk and asked me one question.
Not how long did you work today?
He asked, who is better off because of what you did?
That sentence stayed with me for life.
Asterisk in my family, nobody believes time is the product.
Time is only the cost.
The product is the result.
If you solve a problem for a thousand people,
you are paid like a man who solved it for a thousand people,
even if it took you one afternoon.
If you spend 12 hours doing something nobody needs,
the world pays you almost nothing, and it is not being unfair.
It is being honest.
Asterisk, think of two carpenters.
One builds a single table a day and sells it for a fair price.
The other designs a way to furnish 100 homes.
Both work hard.
Only one is paid for the value he delivers.
Asterisk, most people in America were raised to believe the opposite.
Work more hours and you will learn more.
So they trade their lives by the hour and then wonder why the numbers never grow.
Ashik asks a different question every morning.
Where can I create the most value for the most people?
Change that question and you change your income.
Asterisk number two.
We read and we sit with people older than us.
Asterisk every morning before the first guest arrives I read.
Two hours, sometimes three.
Business history, old trade stories.
The lives of people who built something from nothing.
My grandchildren laugh and say,
Grandfather, you already know everything.
I tell them knowledge works like a deposit.
Each day you add a little and nobody notices.
Then one day you are making decisions that look like magic to everyone around you.
And all you did was read every day for years.
Asterisk wealth follows what you know.
When you understand how markets move, how contracts work and how people think,
you do not need luck.
Yet so many people tell me they are too busy to read for even 20 minutes.
And then they spend three hours looking at a screen.
I am not judging.
I am only showing you where the difference begins.
20 minutes a day.
That is the entrance fee.
Asterisk number three.
We look for the opportunity inside the problem.
Asterisk my grandfather told me a story about two traders
who arrived at a desert village on the same evening.
The first looked around and by morning he was packing his camel.
He told the second trader, do not waste your time.
Nobody in this village owns a lantern.
The second trader stared at him and smiled.
Nobody owns a lantern?
Then every house in this village is a customer.
Asterisk? Same village.
Same night. Same facts.
Two completely different men.
One saw a wall. One saw a door.
Asterisk.
When I meet someone who struggles with money,
I often hear the same sentences.
It is too hard.
There is too much competition.
The market is closed.
When I meet someone who is building wealth,
I hear something else.
What is missing here?
And who would pay to have it solved?
Every problem is a customer waiting for someone brave enough to serve him.
Americans have more freedom to start something than almost anyone on earth.
Still many look at a problem and see only a reason to stop.
Asterisk number four.
We guard who sits in our circle.
Asterisk in Dubai,
the Majolis is the heart of the house.
Everyone who enters it becomes part of your mind for the evening,
so we are careful who sits there.
I welcome everyone with respect,
but I only keep close the people who speak about ideas,
about deals, about learning, about building.
If someone spends the whole night complaining about the government,
the economy and his boss,
I serve him coffee,
I thank him,
and I make sure he is not my daily company.
Asterisk, you become the average of the people you spend the most time with,
and I have watched it happen for 40 years.
A young man who sits with builders starts to think like a builder.
The same young man sitting with people who only complain,
starts to complain and calls it realism.
Asterisk, you do not need to cut anyone off.
You only need to decide on purpose who gets your best hours.
Most people let their circle happen by accident.
Ashik designs it.
Asterisk, those are the first four,
and already you can see the pattern.
None of them cost a single Durham.
They are only choices.
But number five costs something that most people are afraid to spend,
and it is the habit my American guests find hardest to accept.
It is about how you speak about yourself
and why staying quiet is the most expensive mistake of all.
Number five, we speak about our value out loud.
Asterisk, when I was young,
it was a perfumer in our soup who made the finest ood in the whole city.
Everyone who tried it agreed, but he was shy.
He sat behind his table, said nothing,
and waited for people to notice.
Three stalls away, a man with a very average perfume
stood in the middle of the walkway
and told every passerby exactly what he sold,
who it was for and why it was worth the price.
By evening, the loud man had sold out.
The quiet man had sold almost nothing.
My father pointed at them and said,
a diamond in your pocket feeds nobody.
Asterisk, most of my American guests were raised to be modest.
Let your work speak for itself, they say.
But work does not speak.
People speak.
If you do not explain what you offer,
someone with less skill and more courage
will explain it for you and take your customer.
Asterisk, I am not telling you to boast.
A chic never needs to boast.
I am telling you to be clear.
Say what you do.
Say who it helps.
Say your price calmly without apology.
Every month you stay quiet,
you pay a bill that never arrives on paper.
It is the money you never earned
because nobody knew you were worth it.
Asterisk, number six.
We make our goals bigger than our problems.
Asterisk years ago, a man came to my majolise,
tired and worried.
His roof was leaking.
A customer had paid him late and his car needed repairs.
He talked about these things for an hour.
When he finished, I asked him one question.
What do you want to build in the next ten years?
He looked confused.
He had not thought about it in a long time.
Slowly, he described something real.
A business with 40 employees serving a whole region.
And as he spoke, I watched his shoulders change.
When he left, the leaking roof was not a disaster anymore.
It was a Tuesday job.
Asterisk, this is how the mind works.
When your goal is small, small problems look like mountains.
When your goal is large,
the same problems shrink to the size they really are.
Most people spend their whole lives managing their worries
and never once raise their eyes to something worth the trouble.
A chic keeps a very big picture in front of him
so that daily troubles have no room to grow.
Asterisk, now number seven.
This is the one I promised you, Asterisk, a few years ago.
A successful young businessman from America sat in my majlis.
Smart, ambitious, well-dressed.
After coffee, he leaned forward and asked me
what he thought was the most important question of his life.
Chic Umar, he said,
should I focus on earning more money or on spending less?
I smiled and said, both.
He waited for me to continue.
I did not.
He opened his mouth, closed it and looked at the floor.
For almost a full minute, he said nothing at all.
Then he said quietly,
my entire life, everyone told me to pick one.
Asterisk, and that is the point.
Poor thinking is either or.
Rich thinking is both and.
Asterisk, earn more and spend wisely.
Save carefully and invest boldly.
Be generous and stay strong.
Be patient and still move fast when the door opens.
The man who chooses only to save never grows.
The man who chooses only to earn never keeps.
The man who chooses only to give soon has nothing left to give.
Each of those men believes he has found the one true rule.
He has found half of one, Asterisk in my family.
We hold two ideas in the same hand.
We protect what we have and we grow it.
We are careful and we are brave.
When someone tells you that you must choose between two good things, be suspicious.
Often the only thing forcing the choice is a smaller way of thinking.
Ask yourself, what would it look like if I did both?
That question alone has opened more doors for me than any bank ever has.
Asterisk number eight.
We count what we own, not what we earn.
Asterisk, imagine two men.
The first earns a very large salary.
He has a new car, a beautiful watch, a big house with a big loan.
Everyone calls him successful.
The second earns much less.
He drives an old car and wears simple clothes.
But every year, he quietly buys a small piece of something that produces income.
A shop, share of a business, a piece of land.
Asterisk, wait ten years.
Then ask both men one question.
If you stopped working today, how long could you continue?
The first man might last three months.
The second man might last forever.
Asterisk, my grandfather had a saying,
do not be proud of the river, dig the well.
A river is income.
It flows past you and when the rain stops, it disappears.
A well is what you own.
It stays, it fills and it feeds your children and their children.
Asterisk, so on the first day of every month, I do something very simple.
I sit with a small notebook and I write down what I own and what I owe.
Not what I earned, what I own.
Over the years, I have watched that one number tell me more about my life than any paycheck ever could.
If it grows, I am winning, even in a slow year.
If it shrinks, I am losing, even when I feel rich.
Asterisk, most people never look at that number.
They look at their income, feel good or bad about it and move on.
A chic looks at the well.
Asterisk, that is eight.
To remain and they are the ones my guests remember long after they leave.
Number nine is about what we do with money in the first minute after it arrives before we spend a single coin.
And number ten is the quiet habit that holds the other nine together.
It is the most boring one on the list and for that reason, almost everyone skips it.
Do not be one of them.
Number nine, we give the money it's orders the moment it arrives.
Asterisk, when money comes into my house, it does not touch my hands first.
Before I pay a single bill, before I buy anything for myself, I divide it.
One part goes to savings.
One part goes to what I own, to the wells I told you about.
One part goes to giving to people who have less than I do.
Only what remains is for living.
Asterisk, most people do it in the opposite order.
They spend first and hope something is left at the end.
Nothing ever is.
Money that is not given a job before it is spent will always find a job of its own and that job is usually small.
Asterisk, my father taught me this with a simple saying.
The first coin belongs to your future, the second to your community and the third to your table.
When you pay your future first, you never have to chase it.
Asterisk and giving is not a loss.
I have watched it for 40 years.
The families who give steadily are the families who keep their name, their respect and their doors open.
People remember who helped them and the memory comes back to you in ways no bank can promise.
Asterisk now, number 10, the quiet one.
We do all of this for a very long time.
That is the whole secret.
No dramatic move, no single lucky year.
My grandfather planted date palms that he knew would not give fruit for a decade.
When people asked why he bothered, he said, I am not planting for this season.
I am planting for the family that will sit under it.
Asterisk, the man who tries a habit for one month and quits has learned nothing.
The man who repeats a small, sensible habit for 30 years becomes someone his younger self would not recognize.
Reading every morning, counting what he owns on the first of the month, dividing the money before spending it, choosing his circle, none of it is exciting.
All of it together over time becomes a fortune.
Asterisk, this is why wealth stays in my family.
We do not depend on one big decision.
We depend on 10 small ones, repeated every day, handed down from father to son, until they stop feeling like rules and start feeling like who we are.
Asterisk, so now you know what my visitors know?
Be paid for value, not ours.
Read and sit with those who know more.
Find the door inside the problem.
Guard your circle.
Speak clearly about what you offer.
Keep your goals bigger than your troubles.
Hold both ideas, not one.
Count what you own.
Give your money its orders first and do it all patiently for years.
Asterisk, you do not need to be born in Dubai to begin.
You only need to begin today with one habit.
Pick the one that felt the most uncomfortable to hear because that is usually the one you need most.
Asterisk, sit with it tonight and I will see you in the next Majlis.
